title: Why Your Students Need Time To Think
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin argues that a brief, deliberate pause before independent work is a strategy elite performers use but schools never teach: a full stop of sound and movement that lets students plan and visualize a task before touching pencil or keyboard. He contrasts this with the common classroom habit of rushing students straight into production, which he says produces both students who freeze up and students who turn in shoddy work. His prescription is concrete: have students sit still for two to five minutes depending on grade level, think through the objective, and wait for a 'go' signal before beginning. He frames this pause as motivational as well as cognitive, since it builds confidence and excitement about the task ahead. Linsin situates the practice within a broader tradition of contemplation practiced by historical figures, and closes by calling forethought a trainable muscle that must be deliberately cultivated before every creative assignment.
points: Schedule a mandatory thinking pause of two to five minutes before every period of independent or creative work.
During the pause, students may sit still, sketch, or diagram their thinking, but may not begin the actual assignment.
Rushing straight into work without planning causes some students to freeze and others to produce low-quality work.
The pause is not wasted time; students become more efficient and enter a deeper state of flow as they get used to it.
Forethought is a skill that must be deliberately trained and repeated, not a one-time trick.
quotes: It’s a full-stop pause of all activity so students can think . It’s a cessation of sound and movement that enables students to plan, strategize, and visualize the tasks in front of them.
They’ve been conditioned, you see, to begin producing the second they’re given the go-ahead. This is a good thing when it comes to routines and procedures.
Ironically, many of these same students who don’t take the time to think freeze up and take forever to get started. The others simply don’t produce quality work.
The solution to both problems is to require your students to sit and think before putting fingers to keyboard or pencil to paper.
